corrected_value.title: Hippuric Acid in 24-Hour Urine Collections Is a Potential Biomarker for Fruit and Vegetable Consumption in Healthy Children and Adolescents,

decisions.quote:
The observed association between hippuric acid and fruit and 
vegetable intake is also consistent with previous studies con-
ducted in both children [16,55,56] and adults [57–59]. These

decisions.location: Discussion, page 8, lines 1220-1225 (see also Reference [55], page 12, lines 1858-1861, and Discussion, page 9, lines 1401-1404)
decisions.reason: The paper explicitly states in its Abstract Objectives that it aimed to 'screen for potential biomarkers and assess the replicability of previously reported biomarkers associated with fruit and vegetable intake in a free-living population' (lines 113-114). In the Discussion, the authors explicitly frame the fruit/vegetable-hippuric acid association as the previously reported biomarker association that replicated in their study ('Except for the fruit/vegetable-hippuric acid intake association, the other well-documented diet-metabolite associations in adults like proline betaine for citrus fruit intake [73] or phloretin for apple [74] could not be replicated in our study', lines 1401-1404) and compare their positive fruit/vegetable-hippuric acid findings to prior studies in children [16,55,56] (lines 1220-1222). Among [16,55,56], [16] is a systematic review by the present authors and [56] evaluates urinary hippuric acid specifically as a biomarker for dietary flavonoid intake from fruit and vegetables in adolescents, whereas [55] (Krupp, Doberstein, Shi, & Remer, 2012, 'Hippuric acid in 24-hour urine collections is a potential biomarker for fruit and vegetable consumption in healthy children and adolescents') is the primary pediatric study directly reporting the urinary hippuric acid biomarker association with fruit and vegetable consumption. Addressing the blind coder's scope objection: the blind coder relied on lines 1401-1404 to code failed replications of [73] and [74] while dismissing the hippuric acid comparison as mere literature contextualization, which contradicts the opening clause of lines 1401-1404 ('Except for the fruit/vegetable-hippuric acid intake association... could not be replicated in our study') and the Abstract's stated replication objective.

decisions.location: Discussion, page 8, lines 1220-1225 (see also Discussion, page 9, lines 1401-1404)
decisions.reason: The study found positive associations between urinary hippuric acid and short-term apple intake as well as habitual fruit and vegetable intake in the IDEFICS/I.Family cohort (lines 728-731, 970-971) and confirmed positive associations with apple and habitual fruit intake in the DONALD cohort (lines 980-982). Comparing these results to Krupp et al. (2012) [55], the authors conclude that the observed association between hippuric acid and fruit and vegetable intake is consistent with prior pediatric studies [16,55,56] (lines 1220-1225) and explicitly state that '[e]xcept for the fruit/vegetable-hippuric acid intake association, the other well-documented diet-metabolite associations... could not be replicated in our study' (lines 1401-1404). Although the shipped quote from the Abstract combines the within-paper DONALD cohort replication with consistency with prior literature, the primary text directly confirms that the original finding of Krupp et al. (2012) [55] was successfully replicated.

decisions.quote:
Objectives: This exploratory study aimed to screen for potential biomarkers and assess the replicability of previously reported biomarkers 
associated with fruit and vegetable intake in a free-living population.
decisions.location: Abstract, page 1, lines 113-114 (see also Discussion, page 9, lines 1401-1404)
decisions.reason: Both the shipped record and the blind coding classify the record type as 'replication'. While the word 'Replication' in the article title refers to within-paper replication of discovery findings from the IDEFICS/I.Family cohort in the DONALD cohort, the study also uses new pediatric cohort data to test the replicability of previously published urinary biomarkers of fruit and vegetable intake (Abstract, lines 113-114; Discussion, lines 1220-1225, 1401-1404), including the fruit/vegetable-hippuric acid association reported by Krupp et al. (2012) [55].
